topic: Components: batteries, diodes, transistors, tubes, ICs, connectors, ferrites (G6A, G6B; 23 pool questions)

notes.front: What is a lead-acid battery?
notes.back: A rechargeable cell whose electrodes are lead grids in an electrolyte of diluted sulfuric acid.
notes.explanation: It is a common rechargeable cell, familiar from vehicle batteries and standby power supplies.
notes.example: A 12 V car battery is six lead-acid cells connected in series.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 1 glossary: "LEAD-ACID CELL—A cell in an ordinary storage battery, in which electrodes are grids of lead containing an active material consisting of certain lead oxides that change in composition during charging and discharging. The electrodes or plates are immersed in an electrolyte of diluted sulfuric acid."

notes.front: What is a battery's internal resistance?
notes.back: The resistance inside the cell itself, which drops some of the cell's voltage and limits how much current it can deliver.
notes.explanation: A higher internal resistance means more of the cell's own voltage is lost inside it before reaching the load.
notes.example: A battery whose internal resistance rises as it ages can no longer supply the surge of current a starter motor needs.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 1: "The larger the electrodes and the closer together they are ..., the lower the internal resistance of the cell and the more current the cell is capable of supplying to the load."

notes.front: What is a diode's forward threshold voltage?
notes.back: The forward voltage at which a diode begins to conduct significant current.
notes.explanation: Below this voltage the diode conducts almost nothing; above it, current rises rapidly for a small further voltage increase.
notes.example: A silicon diode needs about 0.7 V across it before it starts to conduct.

notes.front: What is germanium?
notes.back: A grayish-white metal having semiconductor properties, symbol Ge, used to make some diodes.
notes.explanation: Germanium diodes have a notably lower forward threshold voltage than silicon diodes.
notes.example: A germanium diode is preferred in some low-signal detector circuits because it starts conducting at a lower voltage.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 7 glossary: "GERMANIUM—A grayish-white metal having semiconductor properties."

notes.front: What is silicon?
notes.back: A metallic element, symbol Si, used in its pure state as a semiconductor.
notes.explanation: Silicon is the most common semiconductor material, used in most diodes, transistors and ICs.
notes.example: Nearly all modern transistors and diodes, other than a few specialist germanium types, are silicon devices.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 7 glossary: "SILICON—A metallic element which, in its pure state, is used as a semiconductor."

notes.front: What is an electrolytic capacitor?
notes.back: A capacitor type offering high capacitance for a given physical volume, commonly used in power supplies.
notes.explanation: Its construction packs a large plate area into a compact package, but it is polarised and must be connected the right way round.
notes.example: The large filter capacitors smoothing the DC output of a linear power supply are usually electrolytic.

notes.front: What is a low-voltage ceramic capacitor?
notes.back: A capacitor type that is comparatively low cost, widely used for small-value RF bypass and coupling jobs.
notes.explanation: It is not chosen for high capacitance or tight tolerance, but for low cost in small values.
notes.example: A small disc-shaped ceramic capacitor bypassing RF around a bias resistor.

notes.front: What is a wire-wound resistor?
notes.back: A resistor made from resistance wire wound on a form, giving accurate values and high current-handling capability.
notes.explanation: The coiled wire has significant inductance, unlike most other resistor types.
notes.example: A wire-wound bleeder resistor across a power supply's filter capacitors.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 1: "Wirewound resistors have very accurate values and possess a higher current handling capability than carbon resistors."

notes.front: What is saturation in a bipolar transistor?
notes.back: The operating state in which the transistor is fully turned on and conducts as much current as the circuit allows.
notes.explanation: Together with cutoff, saturation forms the two operating points used when a transistor is driven as a switch rather than a linear amplifier.
notes.example: A transistor driving an LED is switched into saturation to light it fully.
notes.source: NCVEC 2023–2027 General Pool, G6A07; US Navy NEETS Module 7: "the transistor goes into saturation and cutoff."

notes.front: What is cutoff in a bipolar transistor?
notes.back: The operating state in which the transistor is fully turned off and conducts essentially no current.
notes.explanation: Together with saturation, cutoff forms the two operating points used when a transistor is driven as a switch.
notes.example: A transistor driving an LED is switched into cutoff to turn it off.
notes.source: NCVEC 2023–2027 General Pool, G6A07; US Navy NEETS Module 7: "the transistor goes into saturation and cutoff."

notes.front: What is a MOSFET?
notes.back: A field-effect transistor whose gate is separated from the channel by a thin insulating layer.
notes.explanation: That insulating layer gives a MOSFET an extremely high input impedance at its gate, unlike a bipolar transistor's base.
notes.example: MOSFETs are widely used as RF power amplifier and switching devices because of their high input impedance and low drive requirements.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 7 glossary: "MOSFET—A semiconductor device that contains diffused source and drain regions on either side of a P- or N-channel area. Also contains a gate insulated from the channel area by silicon-oxide."

notes.front: What is a vacuum tube?
notes.back: An electron device in an evacuated envelope, controlling current between a heated cathode and a plate, usually with one or more control grids.
notes.explanation: Vacuum tubes predate transistors and are still used in some high-power amateur amplifiers.
notes.example: A large glass triode or tetrode tube at the heart of a legal-limit HF linear amplifier.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 6: "PLATE CURRENT FLOWS WHEN THE PLATE IS POSITIVE ... PLATE CURRENT IS CUT OFF WHEN THE PLATE IS NEGATIVE."

notes.front: What is the plate of a vacuum tube?
notes.back: The electrode, also called the anode, that collects the electrons flowing from the cathode.
notes.explanation: Current only flows to the plate when it is positive relative to the cathode; a negative plate cuts current off.
notes.example: In a rectifier tube, plate current flows only during the half of the AC cycle when the plate is positive.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 6: "PLATE CURRENT FLOWS WHEN THE PLATE IS POSITIVE ... PLATE CURRENT IS CUT OFF WHEN THE PLATE IS NEGATIVE."

notes.front: What is a vacuum tube's control grid?
notes.back: The electrode nearest the cathode whose signal voltage regulates plate current.
notes.explanation: A small voltage change on the control grid produces a much larger change in plate current, giving the tube its amplifying action.
notes.example: Applying the input signal to the control grid of an amplifier tube produces an amplified version at the plate.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 6 glossary: "CONTROL GRID—The electrode of a vacuum tube, other than a diode, upon which a signal voltage is impressed to regulate the plate current."

notes.front: What is a vacuum tube's screen grid?
notes.back: An extra grid placed between the control grid and the plate to reduce grid-to-plate capacitance.
notes.explanation: Splitting the grid-to-plate capacitance into two series capacitances reduces the total, which curbs unwanted feedback inside the tube.
notes.example: A tetrode tube adds a screen grid to the basic triode structure for this purpose.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 6: "placing an extra grid, called the SCREEN GRID, between the control grid and the plate ... the total interelectrode capacitance between the control grid and the plate is greatly reduced."

notes.front: What is an inductor's self-resonant frequency?
notes.back: The frequency at which an inductor's own stray capacitance resonates with its inductance.
notes.explanation: Every real inductor has some capacitance between its turns, which behaves like a small parallel capacitor.
notes.example: An RF choke used well below its self-resonant frequency behaves as a clean inductor; above it, the choke acts as a capacitor.

notes.front: What is ferrite?
notes.back: A powdered and compressed ferric oxide material that has both magnetic properties and resistance to current flow.
notes.explanation: Different ferrite mixes are optimised for different frequency ranges, which is why the mix matters for performance.
notes.example: A ferrite bead slipped over a coax cable at the antenna feed point.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 11 glossary: "FERRITE—A powdered and compressed ferric oxide material that has both magnetic properties and resistance to current flow."

notes.front: What is a toroid?
notes.back: A doughnut-shaped inductor core, often ferrite, that contains most of its magnetic field within the core itself.
notes.explanation: Because the closed loop shape keeps the field mostly inside the core, a toroidal inductor radiates and picks up less stray coupling than an open rod core.
notes.example: A toroidal ferrite core wound with wire to make an RF choke.

notes.front: What is common-mode current?
notes.back: Unwanted RF current flowing in the same direction on both conductors of a cable, or on a shield, rather than as the intended signal current.
notes.explanation: A ferrite core adds impedance in the path of common-mode current without affecting the wanted signal, whose currents on the two conductors flow in opposite directions and cancel.
notes.example: RF current flowing back down the outside of a coax shield toward the radio is common-mode current.

notes.front: What does MMIC stand for?
notes.back: Monolithic Microwave Integrated Circuit.
notes.explanation: It is a single-chip IC designed to work efficiently at microwave frequencies.
notes.example: A small MMIC amplifier chip used as a low-noise preamplifier on a microwave band.

notes.front: What is CMOS?
notes.back: A family of digital integrated circuits whose main advantage over older bipolar logic families is low power consumption.
notes.explanation: CMOS logic draws very little current when its outputs are not switching, which suits battery-powered equipment.
notes.example: Most modern battery-powered digital electronics uses CMOS logic rather than older bipolar logic families.

notes.front: What is TTL?
notes.back: Transistor-transistor logic: an older family of digital ICs built from bipolar transistors, which draws more power than CMOS.
notes.explanation: TTL logic uses bipolar transistors and typically consumes more current than an equivalent CMOS circuit.
notes.example: Some older digital radio designs use TTL logic chips, now largely superseded by CMOS.

notes.front: What does "analog" mean, as applied to an integrated circuit?
notes.back: Processing signals that vary continuously, as opposed to digital signals that take only discrete values.
notes.explanation: An operational amplifier IC is a classic analog device: its output tracks continuous changes in its input.
notes.example: An op amp IC is classified as analog, in contrast to a digital logic IC.

notes.front: What is an operational amplifier (op amp)?
notes.back: An amplifier IC with very high gain, very high input impedance and very low output impedance, used for computing or signal-transfer operations.
notes.explanation: Those three properties let an op amp's behaviour be shaped almost entirely by the external feedback components around it.
notes.example: An op amp used as an audio speech processor amplifier stage in a transceiver.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 8 glossary: "OPERATIONAL AMPLIFIER (OP AMP)—An amplifier designed to perform computing or transfer operations and which has the following characteristics: (1) very high gain, (2) very high input impedance, and (3) very low output impedance."

notes.front: What does it mean for a diode to be forward biased?
notes.back: An external voltage is applied in the conducting direction, so the junction offers only minimum resistance to current.
notes.explanation: Forward bias is what turns an LED, or any diode, into a conducting device rather than a blocking one.
notes.example: An LED emits light only when it is forward biased.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 7 glossary: "FORWARD BIAS—An external voltage that is applied to a PN junction in the conducting direction so that the junction offers only minimum resistance to the flow of current."

notes.front: What is a BNC connector?
notes.back: A bayonet-locking RF connector with a typical upper frequency limit for low SWR of about 4 GHz.
notes.explanation: Its quick-connect bayonet coupling makes it popular for test equipment and lower-power station wiring.
notes.example: A BNC connector on the antenna input of a handheld VHF/UHF transceiver.

notes.front: What is a type N connector?
notes.back: A moisture-resistant threaded RF connector useful to about 10 GHz.
notes.explanation: Its threaded coupling and weatherproofing suit it to outdoor runs and higher-frequency work than a BNC connector.
notes.example: A type N connector used at the antenna end of a hardline run to a UHF or microwave antenna.

notes.front: What is an SMA connector?
notes.back: A small threaded RF connector suitable for signals up to several GHz.
notes.explanation: Its compact size makes it common on handheld radios and small microwave modules where a full-size N connector would not fit.
notes.example: The antenna connector on most handheld VHF/UHF radios is an SMA connector.

notes.front: What is an RCA phono connector commonly used for?
notes.back: Low frequency or DC signal connections to a transceiver.
notes.explanation: It is not built to hold a steady impedance at radio frequencies, so it is used for audio, keying and DC.
notes.example: The microphone or accessory audio jacks on the back of a transceiver often use RCA phono connectors.

notes.front: What is the minimum allowable discharge voltage for maximum life of a standard 12 V lead-acid battery?
notes.back: 10.5 volts.
notes.explanation: Discharging a lead-acid battery further than this shortens its life and can permanently reduce its capacity.

notes.front: What is the main advantage of a battery with low internal resistance?
notes.back: It can supply a high discharge current.
notes.explanation: Less of the battery's own voltage is lost inside it, so more of its capability reaches the load even under heavy demand.

notes.front: What are the approximate forward threshold voltages of germanium and silicon diodes?
notes.back: Germanium about 0.3 volts; silicon about 0.7 volts.
notes.explanation: The two materials have different band-gap energies, so they need different forward voltages before they start conducting well.

notes.front: How do electrolytic and low-voltage ceramic capacitors differ in their main advantage?
notes.back: Electrolytic: high capacitance for a given volume. Ceramic: comparatively low cost.
notes.explanation: Each type trades off different properties, so the right choice depends on whether the circuit needs large capacitance or just a cheap small value.

notes.front: Why should wire-wound resistors not be used in RF circuits?
notes.back: Their inductance could make circuit performance unpredictable.
notes.explanation: The coil of wire that forms a wire-wound resistor behaves partly as an inductor, which upsets RF circuit behaviour at higher frequencies.

notes.front: What are the two operating points used for a bipolar transistor operated as a switch?
notes.back: Saturation and cutoff.
notes.explanation: A switch needs the transistor to be either fully on or fully off, not partway through its linear range.

notes.front: What distinguishes a MOSFET's construction from other transistors?
notes.back: Its gate is separated from the channel by a thin insulating layer.
notes.explanation: That insulating layer is what gives a MOSFET its extremely high gate input impedance.

notes.front: What do the control grid and screen grid of a vacuum tube each do?
notes.back: Control grid: regulates the flow of electrons between cathode and plate. Screen grid: reduces grid-to-plate capacitance.
notes.explanation: The control grid gives the tube its amplifying action; the screen grid, added in a tetrode, curbs unwanted internal feedback.

notes.front: What happens when an inductor is operated above its self-resonant frequency?
notes.back: It becomes capacitive.
notes.explanation: Above that frequency the inductor's own stray capacitance dominates its behaviour.

notes.front: What sets how a ferrite core performs at different frequencies?
notes.back: Its composition, or "mix": a core material chosen for a particular frequency range.
notes.explanation: The mix determines the frequency range the core works well in.

notes.front: What advantages does a ferrite-core toroidal inductor have?
notes.back: Large inductance, a core mix chosen for the working frequency range, and most of the magnetic field kept inside the core.
notes.explanation: The closed loop shape of a toroid contains the field better than an open rod core.

notes.front: What does the abbreviation MMIC stand for?
notes.back: Monolithic Microwave Integrated Circuit.
notes.explanation: This single term identifies the whole family of small-signal and power chips built for microwave operation.

notes.front: What is CMOS's main advantage over TTL integrated circuits?
notes.back: Low power consumption.
notes.explanation: That low quiescent current is what makes CMOS the usual choice for battery-powered digital circuits.

notes.front: What kind of device is an integrated circuit operational amplifier?
notes.back: Analog.
notes.explanation: An op amp's output tracks a continuously varying input, the defining feature of an analog device.

notes.front: How is an LED biased when it is emitting light?
notes.back: Forward biased.
notes.explanation: Like any diode, an LED conducts and, in its case, emits light only in forward bias.

notes.front: What frequency range or use best suits BNC, type N, SMA and RCA phono connectors?
notes.back: BNC: to about 4 GHz. Type N: moisture-resistant, to about 10 GHz. SMA: small, several GHz. RCA phono: low frequency or DC.
notes.explanation: Each connector trades off size, weatherproofing and upper frequency differently, so the choice depends on the job.
notes.source: NCVEC 2023–2027 General Pool, G6B04, G6B07, G6B11, G6B12

notes.front: Which display device is actually tested from the syllabus item "display devices"?
notes.back: Only the LED, via the pool question on LED bias; no other display device appears in the pool.
notes.explanation: The syllabus lists display devices generally, but the 2023–2027 pool tests only the LED's forward-biased operation.
notes.source: NCVEC 2023–2027 General Pool, syllabus G6B and G6B08

notes.front: What is the minimum allowable discharge voltage for maximum life of a standard 12-volt lead-acid battery?
notes.back: 10.5 volts
notes.choices:
A) 6 volts
B) 8.5 volts
C) 10.5 volts
D) 12 volts
notes.choicesExplained: A and B discharge the battery too deeply, shortening its life. D is the battery's nominal voltage, far above its discharge limit.
notes.explanation: Discharging below 10.5 V shortens the life of a standard 12 V lead-acid battery.

notes.front: What is an advantage of batteries with low internal resistance?
notes.back: High discharge current
notes.choices:
A) Long life
B) High discharge current
C) High voltage
D) Rapid recharge
notes.choicesExplained: A, C and D are not what low internal resistance directly provides; it specifically lets the battery supply a high discharge current without excessive internal voltage loss.
notes.explanation: Less internal voltage drop leaves more of the battery's capability available for a heavy load.

notes.front: What is the approximate forward threshold voltage of a germanium diode?
notes.back: 0.3 volts
notes.choices:
A) 0.1 volt
B) 0.3 volts
C) 0.7 volts
D) 1.0 volts
notes.choicesExplained: A is too low to be a real threshold voltage. C is the silicon, not germanium, threshold. D is higher than either material needs.
notes.explanation: Germanium's lower band-gap energy gives it a lower forward threshold voltage than silicon.

notes.front: Which of the following is characteristic of an electrolytic capacitor?
notes.back: High capacitance for a given volume
notes.choices:
A) Tight tolerance
B) Much less leakage than any other type
C) High capacitance for a given volume
D) Inexpensive RF capacitor
notes.choicesExplained: A and B describe qualities electrolytic capacitors do not excel at. D describes a ceramic capacitor, not an electrolytic one.
notes.explanation: Electrolytic construction packs a large plate area into a small package, giving high capacitance for its size.

notes.front: What is the approximate forward threshold voltage of a silicon junction diode?
notes.back: 0.7 volts
notes.choices:
A) 0.1 volt
B) 0.3 volts
C) 0.7 volts
D) 1.0 volts
notes.choicesExplained: A is too low to be a real threshold voltage. B is the germanium, not silicon, threshold. D is higher than silicon needs.
notes.explanation: Silicon's band-gap energy gives it a forward threshold voltage of about 0.7 V, higher than germanium's.

notes.front: Why should wire-wound resistors not be used in RF circuits?
notes.back: The resistor’s inductance could make circuit performance unpredictable
notes.choices:
A) The resistor’s tolerance value would not be adequate
B) The resistor’s inductance could make circuit performance unpredictable
C) The resistor could overheat
D) The resistor’s internal capacitance would detune the circuit
notes.choicesExplained: A and C are not the specific reason wire-wound resistors are avoided in RF work. D names the wrong reactive property; it is inductance, not capacitance, that is the problem.
notes.explanation: The coiled wire in a wire-wound resistor behaves partly as an inductor at RF, upsetting circuit behaviour.

notes.front: What are the operating points for a bipolar transistor used as a switch?
notes.back: Saturation and cutoff
notes.choices:
A) Saturation and cutoff
B) The active region (between cutoff and saturation)
C) Peak and valley current points
D) Enhancement and depletion modes
notes.choicesExplained: B is the linear-amplifier region, the opposite of switching operation. C and D describe properties of other devices, not a bipolar transistor switch.
notes.explanation: A switch is either fully on (saturation) or fully off (cutoff), never partway through its linear region.

notes.front: Which of the following is characteristic of low voltage ceramic capacitors?
notes.back: Comparatively low cost
notes.choices:
A) Tight tolerance
B) High stability
C) High capacitance for given volume
D) Comparatively low cost
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and C describe strengths of other capacitor types; low voltage ceramic capacitors are chosen mainly for their low cost.
notes.explanation: Ceramic capacitors are simple and cheap to manufacture in small values, which is their main draw.

notes.front: Which of the following describes MOSFET construction?
notes.back: The gate is separated from the channel by a thin insulating layer
notes.choices:
A) The gate is formed by a back-biased junction
B) The gate is separated from the channel by a thin insulating layer
C) The source is separated from the drain by a thin insulating layer
D) The source is formed by depositing metal on silicon
notes.choicesExplained: A describes a junction field-effect transistor's gate, not a MOSFET's. C misplaces the insulating layer between the wrong two elements. D does not describe how a MOSFET's gate is built.
notes.explanation: The insulated gate is the defining feature that gives a MOSFET its very high input impedance.

notes.front: Which element of a vacuum tube regulates the flow of electrons between cathode and plate?
notes.back: Control grid
notes.choices:
A) Control grid
B) Suppressor grid
C) Screen grid
D) Trigger electrode
notes.choicesExplained: B and C are other grids present in some tubes but not the one that regulates plate current. D is not a standard vacuum tube electrode name.
notes.explanation: A signal voltage on the control grid regulates how much current flows from cathode to plate.

notes.front: What happens when an inductor is operated above its self-resonant frequency?
notes.back: It becomes capacitive
notes.choices:
A) Its reactance increases
B) Harmonics are generated
C) It becomes capacitive
D) Catastrophic failure is likely
notes.choicesExplained: A describes normal inductive behaviour below self-resonance, not above it. B and D are not what happens; the inductor simply starts to behave as a capacitor.
notes.explanation: Above self-resonance, the inductor's own stray capacitance dominates its reactance.

notes.front: What is the primary purpose of a screen grid in a vacuum tube?
notes.back: To reduce grid-to-plate capacitance
notes.choices:
A) To reduce grid-to-plate capacitance
B) To increase efficiency
C) To increase the control grid resistance
D) To decrease plate resistance
notes.choicesExplained: B, C and D describe effects that are not the screen grid's primary purpose, which is specifically to split and reduce interelectrode capacitance.
notes.explanation: Placing the screen grid between control grid and plate splits their capacitance into two series capacitances, reducing the total.

notes.front: What determines the performance of a ferrite core at different frequencies?
notes.back: The composition, or “mix,” of materials used
notes.choices:
A) Its conductivity
B) Its thickness
C) The composition, or “mix,” of materials used
D) The ratio of outer diameter to inner diameter
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and D are physical properties, but it is the ferrite mix, not these, that determines the useful frequency range.
notes.explanation: Different ferrite mixes are formulated for different frequency ranges.

notes.front: What is meant by the term MMIC?
notes.back: Monolithic Microwave Integrated Circuit
notes.choices:
A) Multi-Mode Integrated Circuit
B) Monolithic Microwave Integrated Circuit
C) Metal Monolayer Integrated Circuit
D) Mode Modulated Integrated Circuit
notes.choicesExplained: A, C and D are plausible-sounding but incorrect expansions of the same four letters.
notes.explanation: MMIC names a single-chip IC built for efficient microwave-frequency operation.

notes.front: Which of the following is an advantage of CMOS integrated circuits compared to TTL integrated circuits?
notes.back: Low power consumption
notes.choices:
A) Low power consumption
B) High power handling capability
C) Better suited for RF amplification
D) Better suited for power supply regulation
notes.choicesExplained: B, C and D are not the recognised advantage of CMOS over TTL, which is specifically its much lower quiescent power draw.
notes.explanation: CMOS logic draws very little current when its outputs are not switching, unlike TTL.

notes.front: What is a typical upper frequency limit for low SWR operation of 50-ohm BNC connectors?
notes.back: 4 GHz
notes.choices:
A) 50 MHz
B) 500 MHz
C) 4 GHz
D) 40 GHz
notes.choicesExplained: A and B understate a BNC connector's real upper limit. D overstates it; that range needs a connector better suited to microwave use.
notes.explanation: A BNC connector keeps a low SWR up to about 4 GHz, adequate for HF through low microwave use.

notes.front: What is an advantage of using a ferrite core toroidal inductor?
notes.back: All these choices are correct
notes.choices:
A) Large values of inductance may be obtained
B) The magnetic properties of the core may be optimized for a specific range of frequencies
C) Most of the magnetic field is contained in the core
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and C are each individually true of a ferrite toroidal inductor, but each names only one advantage, so the complete answer is D.
notes.explanation: A toroidal ferrite core delivers large inductance, a core material chosen for a particular frequency range, and good field containment all at once.

notes.front: What kind of device is an integrated circuit operational amplifier?
notes.back: Analog
notes.choices:
A) Digital
B) MMIC
C) Programmable Logic
D) Analog
notes.choicesExplained: A and C describe digital circuit families, not an op amp's continuous-signal operation. B names a different device category entirely.
notes.explanation: An op amp processes continuously varying signals, the defining trait of an analog device.

notes.front: Which of the following describes a type N connector?
notes.back: A moisture-resistant RF connector useful to 10 GHz
notes.choices:
A) A moisture-resistant RF connector useful to 10 GHz
B) A small bayonet connector used for data circuits
C) A low noise figure VHF connector
D) A nickel plated version of the PL-259
notes.choicesExplained: B describes a different connector type, not the type N. C and D are not accurate descriptions of a type N connector.
notes.explanation: A type N connector's threaded, weatherproof design suits it to outdoor use up to about 10 GHz.

notes.front: How is an LED biased when emitting light?
notes.back: Forward biased
notes.choices:
A) In the tunnel-effect region
B) At the Zener voltage
C) Reverse biased
D) Forward biased
notes.choicesExplained: A and B describe operating regions used by other kinds of diodes, not an emitting LED. C is the opposite bias direction; an LED does not emit light reverse biased.
notes.explanation: Like any diode, an LED conducts, and in its case emits light, only when forward biased.

notes.front: How does a ferrite bead or core reduce common-mode RF current on the shield of a coaxial cable?
notes.back: By creating an impedance in the current’s path
notes.choices:
A) By creating an impedance in the current’s path
B) It converts common-mode current to differential mode current
C) By creating an out-of-phase current to cancel the common-mode current
D) Ferrites expel magnetic fields
notes.choicesExplained: B, C and D describe mechanisms that are not how a ferrite works; a ferrite simply adds impedance in the common-mode current's path, without converting or actively cancelling it.
notes.explanation: The ferrite's added impedance opposes the common-mode current specifically, while leaving the wanted signal current largely unaffected.

notes.front: What is an SMA connector?
notes.back: A small threaded connector suitable for signals up to several GHz
notes.choices:
A) A type-S to type-M adaptor
B) A small threaded connector suitable for signals up to several GHz
C) A connector designed for serial multiple access signals
D) A type of push-on connector intended for high-voltage applications
notes.choicesExplained: A, C and D are invented-sounding descriptions that do not match a real SMA connector.
notes.explanation: An SMA connector's small threaded body suits compact radios and modules working up to several GHz.

notes.front: Which of these connector types is commonly used for low frequency or dc signal connections to a transceiver?
notes.back: RCA Phono
notes.choices:
A) PL-259
B) BNC
C) RCA Phono
D) Type N
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and D are RF connectors chosen for their frequency performance, not the usual choice for low-frequency or DC accessory connections.
notes.explanation: RCA phono connectors are not built to hold a steady impedance at radio frequencies, so they are used for audio, keying and DC.

notes.front: How do germanium and silicon diodes differ in forward threshold voltage?
notes.back: Germanium is lower, about 0.3 V; silicon is higher, about 0.7 V.
notes.explanation: Mixing these up is the most common way to miss a threshold-voltage question, since the pool tests both values.

notes.front: How do electrolytic and ceramic capacitors differ in their main selling point?
notes.back: Electrolytic wins on high capacitance per volume; ceramic wins on low cost.
notes.explanation: Neither type is chosen for tight tolerance; each is picked for a different practical reason.

notes.front: How do saturation and cutoff differ as transistor switch states?
notes.back: Saturation: fully on, maximum current flows. Cutoff: fully off, essentially no current flows.
notes.explanation: A switching transistor is driven between these two extremes and normally never lingers in its linear region between them.

notes.front: How do CMOS and TTL logic families differ?
notes.back: CMOS draws very little quiescent current; TTL, built from bipolar transistors, draws considerably more power.
notes.explanation: That power difference, not speed or capability, is the one the pool asks about directly.

notes.front: How do BNC, type N and SMA connectors compare in typical frequency range and use?
notes.back: BNC: bayonet, to about 4 GHz. Type N: threaded, weatherproof, to about 10 GHz. SMA: small threaded, several GHz, compact gear.
notes.explanation: Choosing the wrong one for a frequency or environment is a common error on connector questions.
notes.source: NCVEC 2023–2027 General Pool, G6B04, G6B07, G6B11
